# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

LED driver systems are widely used in lighting, displays, automotive applications, and many embedded systems. In modern aircraft cabins, almost all lighting is now LED-based, from the ceiling and sidewall lighting to the reading lamps. These systems must be energy efficient, have a long lifetime and withstand vibration and shock [@lumileds2015]. The weight and the power consumption of the lighting system are important, because they increase the fuel consumption of the aircraft [@krellera2009]. If every segment of the cabin is controlled by its own lines from a central driver, the number of wires grows with every segment that is added. A scalable approach that reduces this complexity is called as **daisy-chainable segment** concept, in which each segment receives data, uses the part meant for itself, and passes the remaining data to the next segment [@aes_wishlist]. Such segments are often built with mixed-signal LED drivers combine analog current-driving circuits with digital control logic. The digital part is responsible for controlling these LED-based systems.

"AES GmbH" develops products and services for the aerospace and maritime industry, from LED lighting systems and power supplies to communication and information systems for aircraft cabins [@aes_website]. AES is currently working on making its analog circuits and digital logic more efficient. This thesis focuses on the digital control part of such a lighting system, in particular the communication between daisy-chained LED segments using a **Cologne Chip GateMate FPGA**, which is developed in Germany [@eenews_gatemate], and a fully open-source design flow consisting of **Yosys, nextpnr and openFPGALoader** [@shah2019; @openfpgaloader].

## Motivation and Challenges

An airline can create different *light effects* for each phase of a flight with *red, green, blue and white (RGBW)* LEDs, for instance a bright, neutral light for boarding, a warm light during the meal service, and a dim, blue light at night [@lumileds2015]. All these segments should change their colour and brightness simultaneously to avoid *visible flicker*. This is achieved by sending the brightness values to all segments over a digital communication line by a *central controller*. 

Electronics for aircraft must also be *reliable and cost-effective*. Each extra component adds cost and a possible point of failure. In the present AES design, each RGBW segment is controlled by an STM32 microcontroller, which receives commands over UART and generates the PWM signals to control LED channels connected to it. My work examines whether a GateMate FPGA from Cologne Chip can take over this task. Using this for communication reduces cost and point of failures by handling **more than one** RGBW segment. The main topic is communication between the nodes using the AES's own protocol called **FlexLink**, each FPGA node receives the data sent by the master, keeps the brightness values for its own segments, and forwards the remaining data to the next node. The design is first modelled in MATLAB/Simulink, then written in Verilog, and finally tested on two GateMate evaluation boards, with a PC acting as the master and low-side MOSFETs switching the LEDs. 

### Problem statement

For the daisy-chain to work, every node in the chain has to do four things at the same time. It has to take the brightness values that belong to its own segment out of the packet and pass the rest on to the next node. It has to turn its own values into pulse-width modulation (PWM) signals for the red, green, blue and white LEDs. And it has to answer the master, for example with its identification number and its temperature. @fig-system-architecture shows this chain in the prototype of this thesis.

![System architecture of the prototype: PC master, USB-TTL adapter and two daisy-chained GateMate nodes. Blue = uplink (master to segments), red = downlink (segments to master), green = PWM to the LED segment.](images/ch1_system_architecture){#fig-system-architecture width=100%}

The difficulty lies in the timing. Each node adds a small delay before the data reaches the next one, and in a chain these delays add up. Even so, the 25th segment has to receive its new values within 25 ms, so that a passenger does not see the light change from one end of the cabin to the other. At the same time, the brightness must be set with 16-bit resolution and the PWM frequency must stay above 400 Hz to avoid visible flicker [@aes_wishlist]. These requirements are clear on paper, but it is not obvious how a small digital circuit can meet all of them at once, while every node in the chain runs exactly the same design.

This leads to the question of this thesis. **Can the control and forwarding part of such a daisy-chained RGBW LED node be built as one small FPGA design that meets the timing of the chain, and can this be shown on real hardware using only open-source tools?**

## Objectives {#sec-objectives}

The main objective of this thesis is to follow the requirements given by AES [@aes_digital_requirements] which includes one FPGA can do the work of a daisy-chained RGBW LED node and meet the timing of the AES concept. Mainly, the design should reach a dimming resolution of 16 bits with a PWM frequency above 400 Hz, update a chain of 25 segments within the limit of 25 ms, and run same logic on every node, so that the nodes can be added to the chain without any changes. It should be built with open-source tools only and be written in a way that it could later move to an ASIC. The objective is reached when these points are shown not only by calculation and simulation, but also by measurements on a real chain of GateMate boards.

Besides this result, the thesis is also a chance for me to learn the complete flow of digital hardware design in practice, how the timing of a serial protocol is turned into working logic, how an open-source tool flow takes a Verilog design to a running FPGA, and how real signals are measured and understood with an oscilloscope when they do not look the same as in the simulation.

## Scope of the Thesis {#sec-scope}

The thesis covers the digital part of the LED driver concept of AES, the serial communication with the Flexlink protocol, the forwarding of data along the chain, the automatic numbering of the nodes, the responses to the master and the generation of the 16-bit PWM signals but not the analog part which are, 18 V to 36 V DC-DC converter, the voltage level shifting of the data line, LED driver stage, and the regulation of the current by using potentiometer for each channel. The design of an ASIC is also not part of the work, but the Verilog code is written so that it could later move to an ASIC flow.

To fit the work into the time of a Master's thesis, the prototype is simplified. The chain consists of two GateMate boards instead of 25 segments, so the behaviour of a longer chain is calculated from the measured delay per node. A PC takes the role of the master, each node drives one RGBW segment, the temperature in the answer is a fixed value, and the LEDs are switched by a simple LED driver stage (MOSFETS) without current regulation. These simplifications and their effect on the results are discussed in @sec-eval-limitations.

## Methodology {#sec-methodology}

The work follows the **V-model**, which is often used for the development of electronic systems (@fig-v-model). The left side of the V describes the design from the top down which are system requirements (@sec-requirements), the system architecture and the Simulink model (@sec-requirements, @sec-simulink), and the Verilog modules of the RTL design (@sec-rtl). At the bottom of the V, the design is implemented with the open-source tool flow Yosys, nextpnr and openFPGALoader. The right side verifies the design from the bottom up, and each test checks the design level on the same height on the left. The Verilog modules are checked by module and system testbenches in Icarus Verilog (@sec-rtl), the system architecture by the hardware tests on the GateMate boards (@sec-hardware), and the requirements by the final evaluation (@sec-evaluation).

In practice, the phases are partly overlapped. The requirements and the Simulink model were worked out first, then the Flexlink node was written in Verilog and it was loaded into two GateMate boards and tested with a Python program on the PC and measured output in a PicoScope oscilloscope. The code and the documentation were kept under version control in Git.

![V-model of this thesis: each design level on the left is verified by the matching test level on the right.](images/ch1_v_model){#fig-v-model width=85%}

## Structure of the Thesis {#sec-structure}

@sec-fundamentals explains the basics the work builds on, from LEDs and PWM dimming to FPGAs, serial communication and the Flexlink protocol. @sec-requirements collects the requirements, analyses the timing of the chain and explains the design decisions. @sec-simulink describes the Simulink model of the data path, and @sec-rtl presents the Verilog design of the Flexlink node and its simulation. @sec-hardware shows the prototype and the measurements, and @sec-evaluation compares the results with the requirements and discusses the limits of the work. @sec-conclusion closes the thesis with a summary and an outlook.
